Photograph: Luke MacGregor/Reuters Mohamed Al Fayed At least five Mohamed Al Fayed abuse survivors confirmed as human-trafficking victims Decision comes after group of survivors claimed ex-Harrods owner’s associates must have helped facilitate his crimes Helena Horton Sun 2 Aug 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least five victims of the former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed have been confirmed by the Home Office as victims of human trafficking. A group of survivors of abuse by the deceased businessman had called for the Metropolitan police to make trafficking the main focus of its investigation, arguing that Fayed could not have committed his offences without a steady stream of women sent to him by associates. The women were victims of international and domestic trafficking, and one survivor told the Press Association (PA) they were recruited to a false role within Harrods . Two further victims were hired for a legitimate role and then selected from the shop floor for abuse. These cases stretch from the 1990s to the most recent, which took place after the 2010 sale of Harrods. Officers are looking into who may have facilitated Fayed’s crimes, in an investigation known as Operation Cornpoppy. Four people have been questioned to date, 21 months after the investigation opened. One survivor, known as Justine, told PA she felt “shellshocked” when she received the conclusive grounds decision in June that she had been a victim of modern slavery. She added: “But it’s a really significant thing, getting that decision, seeing it in writing that you were a victim of modern slavery and trafficking is very … it’s really shocking to read.” Another survivor, Isabella, who worked in the chair’s office at Harrods in 2001, told PA: “He couldn’t have done what he did without Harrods processing women to him and silencing them afterwards. It wasn’t just Harrods, obviously. It was any entity that Fayed owned or had control of. It was his yachts, his aviation business, the Ritz Paris, his properties all over France and Monaco. It went as far as the States and the UAE – anywhere that man touched.” More than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Fayed for the period between 1977 and 2014 – including claims of rape, sexual assault, human trafficking, false imprisonment, drugging, physical violence and forced abortions. The Egyptian businessman died in 2023 aged 94, without facing any charges. A woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Fayed previously came forward to say she had been trafficked in Paris on his orders in 2008 before being sent to London to be sexually assaulted by him. Pelham Spong, 40, from South Carolina in the US, said Fayed, who owned the Ritz hotel in Paris, had forcibly kissed her and offered her a salary of € 65,000 a year if she slept with him. Victims have previously complained of how the Metropolitan police have handled the investigations into Fayed’s abuse. The Independent Office for Police Conduct is examining complaints about the force’s handling of allegations between 2018 and 2024. A Harrods spokesperson said: “Harrods supports all survivors in their pursuit of justice and continues to work closely with the Met police on its investigation”. Photograph: EYE4images/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Raheem Sterling Raheem Sterling charged with dangerous driving and nitrous oxide possession Former England forward crashed on M3 in late May Sterling is also accused of failing to provide a specimen PA Media Wed 26 Aug 2026 04.34 EDT Last modified on Wed 26 Aug 2026 06.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The former England forward Raheem Sterling has been charged with dangerous driving and possession of nitrous oxide after a crash involving a Lamborghini on the motorway, police have said. Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said the charges followed a single-vehicle collision on the M3 southbound, near Minley interchange, on 28 May. The 31-year-old is accused of dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen. The force said that no other vehicles were involved in the collision and no injuries were reported. Sterling, from Berkshire, is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court for a hearing on 15 September. Quick Guide How do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts? Show In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications. If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version. If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'. He scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate’s side to reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the Euro 2020 final. Sterling came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut and moved in 2015 to Manchester City, with whom he won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the FA Cup. Sterling left for Chelsea in 2022 but after falling out of favour he spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal. After leaving Stamford Bridge, he joined the Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of last season. He is now without a club. In the 2021 Queen’s birthday honours, Sterling was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out strongly against racism on and off the pitch. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Kemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA View image in fullscreen Kemi Badenoch measures up Andrew Griffith, her newly appointed shadow chancellor, for a shirt in December last year. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA Conservatives Conservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team? From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players Andrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffle Helena Horton and Harry Cockburn Mon 31 Aug 2026 14.45 EDT Last modified on Mon 31 Aug 2026 15.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google K emi Badenoch has kicked off the return to parliament with a reshuffle of her top team in order to take on Andy Burnham and Reform UK. She has made sweeping changes to the shadow cabinet and ruthlessly axed her shadow chancellor. Here is a run-down of the new characters sitting across from Labour on the opposition frontbench. Andrew Griffith Griffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, replaces Mel Stride as shadow chancellor, a role he has reportedly long coveted. He is loyal to Badenoch and was one of her first backers for leader in 2024. Previously the chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Sky and the chair of Just Eat, he entered parliament as an ally of Boris Johnson after allowing the former prime minister to use his £9.5m townhouse as his leadership campaign HQ in 2019. He later became Johnson’s business adviser in government before running for election later that year. Griffith was a backer of Liz Truss for leader and as her treasury minister was partially responsible for the disastrous mini-budget which caused economic chaos. He continued to defend the budget and said the market turmoil was linked to global events. He was spotted last year at the launch of a climate denial group with Truss and Nigel Farage. Of his attendance, he said: “In any year, I attend hundreds of external events with business organisations and thinktanks, none of which automatically imply my endorsement.” He also recently spoke at a hard-right Cpac event organised by Truss. Claire Coutinho Widely tipped as one of the party’s rising stars, Coutinho made a fierce opponent to Ed Miliband when he was energy secretary and she shadowed his brief. A cabinet minister in Rishi Sunak’s government, she has been shifted to Badenoch’s economic unit and made shadow business secretary. Before parliament she was an investment banker at Merrill Lynch and KPMG, and has recently been holding the Labour government’s feet to the fire over rising energy bills. View image in fullscreen Claire Coutinho. Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty Images Colleagues describe her as forensic, she delights in doing her own research about what she terms “the hidden cost of net zero” and has spoken up in parliament for whistleblowers at the national energy systems operator. She became the first person to represent a political party at PMQs while pregnant earlier this year. Julia Lopez, the MP for Hornchurch and Upminster, will cover for her until the new year while she is on maternity leave. Coutinho is a keen cook in her spare time and once appeared on Nigella Lawson’s cooking gameshow The Taste. Tom Tugendhat Badenoch has made a show of purging the more “woke” MPs from the party, banning those who believe in pursuing net zero from standing at the next election for example, so the choice of the moderate Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary surprised some. View image in fullscreen Tom Tugendhat. Photograph: House of Commons/PA He replaces Priti Patel, who was sacked from the shadow cabinet. Tugendhat has experience in foreign affairs and previously served in the cabinet as security minister from September 2022 to July 2024. A former British army officer, he served in Afghanistan and Iraq. A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch. Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024. He was banned from driving for six months in 2022 for using his mobile phone at the wheel. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Katie Lam A darling of the Tory right, Lam was only elected in 2024. She has been given the role of shadow housing and communities minister, and is likely to relish being Angela Rayner’s opposite number. She is a former special adviser to Johnson, and she worked on Sunak’s first leadership bid. Outside politics she worked at the PR company Portland Communications and the AI company Faculty. View image in fullscreen Katie Lam. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images She has sometimes been tipped as a potential defector to Reform after saying many immigrants should “go home” and supporting the policy of revoking indefinite leave to remain. Her comments on immigration have gone further than official Conservative policy at some points. Lam has written five musicals, including an adaptation of The Railway Children. Other changes and those staying on Chris Philp remains shadow home secretary. He supported Badenoch’s successful leadership campaign and has held the role since she became party leader. James Cartlidge stays on as shadow defence secretary, a position he has held since Sunak appointed him to the role in 2024. Andrew Bowie takes up Coutinho’s previous role as energy secretary. The shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, quit the frontbench to “focus on constituency work”, and Damian Hinds assumes his brief. https://www.politico.eu/article/romania-.text: Romanian President Nicușor Dan faces demands from allies and adversaries alike to call a snap election, the first in the country’s modern history, if his latest attempt to end five months of political paralysis fails. The key NATO and EU member has lacked a fully functioning government since the coalition collapsed in May, and lawmakers have rejected a succession of Dan’s prime ministerial nominees. Political parties are now weighing up whether to support Dan’s latest prime ministerial candidate, the diplomat Luca Niculescu, who must win a confidence vote in parliament within the next nine days to be confirmed in the role. Advertisement Advertisement In an interview, Dan’s arch-rival on Romania’s hard right, George Simion, warned that no stable government can form without an election and accused the president of mounting a “blockade” against democracy because he is “afraid of us coming to power.” Speaking separately to POLITICO, Dan’s most recently defeated candidate for prime minister, Member of the European Parliament Siegfried Mureșan, warned the country was already paying an economic price, with investment decisions being delayed. “Postponing early elections and staying in this stalemate situation would, at some point, also have economic negative consequences,” he said. Bordering Ukraine, Romania has the sixth-largest population in the EU and plays a critical role in NATO’s defense of the region as home to a major military base and a U.S. missile shield site. The country has been plagued by political instability, corruption and a ballooning budget deficit in recent years, conditions that have fueled a surge in support for hard-right nationalist politics. Since the coalition fell apart amid infighting over budget cuts in the spring, Romania’s deadlocked parliament has been unable to agree on a new government. Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) leader Simion, a staunch euroskeptic who has called for a halt to aid for Ukraine, told POLITICO the president must face his duty and give voters a chance to end the stalemate with a fresh election, or face being ousted. His party has been leading Romania’s opinion polls for almost two years. Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president, which he believes will gain momentum if Niculescu fails and Dan again refuses to call fresh elections. Advertisement Advertisement “Everybody says, ‘OK, if this won’t pass, we will go to snap elections,’ but they do not know Nicușor Dan as I do,” Simion said. The president is “very stubborn” and could defy calls for elections even if all parties want them, he said. “In that case we will have the numbers of signatures and votes to suspend him at least, if not sack him.” Dan has refused to contemplate handing AUR a role in government. He defeated Simion for the presidency last year and regards his rival’s politics as a threat to Romania’s pro-Western, pro-European direction . The president says he opposes a snap election because the campaign period would delay budget reforms and healthcare funding. ‘A new Greece’ The Romanian leu has weakened against the euro in the months since the crisis blew up. Simion urged international investors to remain patient and sought to reassure them that AUR would be fiscally responsible if it won power. “Nobody wants a new Greece,” he said. “We will do everything it takes to respect our commitments to our international partners and for them to recover the debts.” The call for an early election is gaining traction in Bucharest. So far, the leader of Dan’s former party, the Save Romania Union, has joined politicians from the National Liberal Party, and the leader of the Social Democratic Party and AUR, in suggesting an unprecedented emergency election could be required. George Simion has been building support in parliament to censure the president. | Robert Ghement/EPA Dan’s latest plan still has time to work, but political feuding between parties remains a problem. The Liberals say they could support Niculescu as prime minister if the Social Democrats do not get too much influence, while the Social Democrats say they want the PM-designate to take the country in a new direction — away from the austerity policies of the outgoing Liberal premier, Ilie Bolojan. Advertisement Advertisement Mureșan, a pro-EU Liberal and European People’s Party vice-president, said the economic risks of prolonging the crisis were real. He told POLITICO a snap election could be inevitable, though this is not his “preferred” option. “The political uncertainty which exists now in the country can easily transform into economic uncertainty,” Mureșan warned. “We are already now seeing investors holding back on their investments, waiting with major investment decisions before they have more certainty.” While Mureșan said he wants Dan to succeed, he criticized the delays in resolving the longest-running crisis since the fall of communism in 1989. “Had the president moved fast in appointing a prime minister in May and not delayed the nominations, we might even have had early elections [by] now, and we would be in a situation with a new parliament, and with a stable government with the four-year agenda,” he said. “So, clearly, the options are narrowing down and are not getting better, following the prolongation of the political crisis.”

https://www.emsnow.com/behind-the-us-lit.text: Behind the US-Lithuania deal: why the US needs more advanced lasers September 25, 2026 Analysis , Artificial Intelligence , Europe , Materials for electronic assembly , PCB Vilnius. Last week, the US and Lithuania signed a deal for critical minerals, aiming to reduce both countries’ dependency on single suppliers and potentially create partnerships in areas such as photonics. According to Lithuanian femtosecond laser company LITILIT, such a partnership could significantly contribute to boosting the growing US industries such as semiconductors and data centers. During the meeting , the US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Lithuania is a global leader in photonics and called Lithuania a photonic power, highlighting Lithuania’s competences in the field. Meanwhile, the Lithuanian Foreign Affairs Minister Kęstutis Budrys noted that Lithuania could increase exports of femtosecond lasers to the US and potentially form a decade-long partnership. According to Nikolajus Gavrilinas, CEO of Lithuanian femtosecond laser company LITILIT, such a partnership could give an economic stimulus to the US’s growing industries. “Femtosecond lasers, due to their extreme precision and ability to delicately process materials, are increasingly used in advanced packaging of semiconductors, as well as in making equipment for optical components powering modern AI data centers, such as glass substrates. As the demand for these multi-billion industries grows, so will the demand for femtosecond lasers,” Gavrilinas says. The growing demand for precision manufacturing is already visible across US industry. Intel recently announced a partnership for precision laser glass processing capability to build its new glass substrate packaging for AI chips, while Nvidia earlier this year backed Corning to expand US manufacturing of optical connectivity components for AI data centers. Femtosecond lasers are also widely used in medical applications, including ophthalmic surgery, as well as in high-precision electronics manufacturing. Meeting that demand at scale is exactly where Gavrilinas sees Lithuania’s opening. “Even though Lithuania is a relatively small country, it has been developing its lasers for 60 years and is one of the world’s several leading laser hubs. It has both the science and the technology to produce world-leading lasers,” Gavrilinas says. “Another important factor is that Lithuania can produce these lasers at scale, which is typically very difficult, as manufacturing femtosecond lasers often requires a high level of skilled employees.” LITILIT is currently finishing development of a femtosecond laser factory in Vilnius that, according to Gavrilinas, is on track to be the highest capacity in the world. The company builds lasers on two patented technologies ( patent 1 , patent 2 ): one invented by LITILIT co-founder Kęstutis Regelskis with Gediminas Račiukaitis of the Center for Physical Sciences and Technology (FTMC), the other developed at LITILIT by Nerijus Rusteika, Ildar Galin, Regelskis and Nikolajus Gavrilinas. The company’s lasers also rely on a purpose-built architecture, significantly reduced component complexity and a high level of production automation, which, according to Gavrilinas, allows it to approach femtosecond laser manufacturing differently from traditional production methods and scale production quickly. During the first year after the launch, the company plans to manufacture 1,000 lasers a year, and then scale towards 3,000 lasers per year as the factory reaches full capacity. In comparison, last year global production capacity of femtosecond lasers was only 9,600 units, according to Reports and Markets. “Later, we plan to replicate our factory model with international partners in other regions, and the US is at the top of that list. Its semiconductor and AI industries are growing faster than almost anywhere else, and we want Lithuania to be part of that growth for decades to come,” Gavrilinas concludes. https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA View image in fullscreen More than three-quarters of consultants who took part in the BMA ballot voted in favour of strike action. Photograph: Jeff Moore/PA NHS NHS consultants to go on two-day strike in England in November Industrial action by senior doctors to begin on 25 November with only emergency cover provided, BMA says Denis Campbell Health policy editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.05 EDT First published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google England’s most senior hospital doctors will strike next month in a dispute over their pay and hours, prompting NHS bosses to warn that patients will suffer “pain, discomfort and inconvenience”. Consultant doctors, who earn an average of £152,000 a year inclusive of overtime and merit awards, will stage a two-day walkout on 25 and 26 November, as hospitals gear up for the extra pressures winter brings. On those days, hospitals will operate with consultants providing only emergency cover, in the way they do on Christmas Day, because most will withdraw their labour. Consultants decided to strike after 18 months of talks with the government did not lead to agreement on key issues, including their call for action to address a 25% fall in the real-terms value of their salaries since 2009-10, the British Medical Association (BMA) said. The senior doctors also want a 10% cut in their working hours. The BMA accused ministers of ignoring consultants’ concerns about burnout related to their workloads and said last week’s well-below-inflation pay offer of a 2.4% increase for next year was the last straw. Consultants voted in July to take industrial action. The BMA said that since then, informal talks with the Department of Health and Social Care had produced no meaningful progress, only another cut to the value of their pay. View image in fullscreen Consultant doctors last went on strike in 2023, when they walked out for nine days. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Ciarán Devane, the head of the NHS Alliance, which represents NHS leaders, said he was “astonished and dismayed” by the BMA’s move at a time when the health service was working to tackle a backlog of more than 6 million patients awaiting more than 7m treatments. “NHS leaders will be both astonished and dismayed by the BMA’s decision to proceed with walkouts by consultants at a time when plans to restore waiting time targets hang by a thread and as teams make wider preparations for winter after a gruelling summer,” Devane said. “Any decision to down tools risks throwing these plans further off course and will once again disrupt patient care while severely hitting NHS finances. “A consultant walkout will result in non-urgent outpatient appointments, elective surgeries and follow-ups being postponed or rescheduled. While [postponement] is needed in the interests of patient safety, it will potentially leave patients in unnecessary pain, discomfort, and inconvenience.” The BMA’s decision presents the prime minister, Andy Burnham, with a considerable challenge as he grapples with tight public finances and Labour’s aim of improving access to NHS care. In June, resident doctors – formerly known as junior doctors – accepted a deal to end a campaign of strikes that had lasted more than three years. Consultants last staged stoppages in 2023, when they walked out for nine days during four strikes. “Since we entered into dispute over 18 months ago we have engaged in good faith with the government, proposing practical solutions,” said Dr Helen Neary and Dr Shanu Datta, the co-chairs of the BMA’s consultants committee. “But time and time again ministers have kicked the can down the road. Unfortunately, that road has now run out, and we have been forced to announce strikes. “Consultants take their responsibilities incredibly seriously, and striking does not come naturally, but we are hearing loud and clear from the profession that they have had enough. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “Not only is our pay still a quarter down in real terms on what it was 17 years ago, having fallen more steeply than the rest of the economy, but we are also not being given time to dedicate our all to the NHS and patients, with quality and improvement being traded for the treadmill of target-chasing, driving colleagues to burnout through excessive workloads.” Ben Morrin, the chief executive of NHS Employers, which represents England’s 205 health trusts, urged the BMA to be realistic about what size of pay rise was affordable. “We need to be honest and transparent about what the NHS can afford at this time. If that limit is reached and industrial action takes place, we owe it to patients to focus on delivering the safest care we can,” he said. He added that the strike would “weaken the clinical teams in every NHS hospital, which are essential to delivering high-quality patient care this winter”. Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, urged consultants to “not take irresponsible action that would place our health service under even greater pressure” during what would be a tough winter for the NHS. A Department of Health and Social Care source said: “The BMA’s consultants committee is threatening strikes because they want a five-hour cut to the working week and to reduce the proportion of their week spent treating patients, changes that would cost taxpayers over £2bn.
